In October, the OSI hosted the State of the Source track at All Things Open designed to connect developers with the big policy conversations shaping our ecosystem. Jonathan Starr, Executive Director of the Open Source Endowment, led “Is Open Source Dying? Short film and open discussion.”

Is Open Source Dying? Short film and open discussion

The idea that AI could end Open Source is provocative, but it distracts from the real issue: sustainability. This short film and open discussion explores how foundations, funding platforms, grants, and corporate contributions can evolve to support maintainers and build a more resilient Open Source ecosystem in the age of AI.

Video Transcript

Nick Vidal: All right. So, the title of this session, “Saving Open Source in the Era of AI,” is kind of provocative, right? I mean, is AI going to be killing open source or is it going to help? So, in your view, Jonathan, what are we actually trying to save?

Jonathan Starr: I think you put it well with the community. We’re trying to save the community. If you have all these AI agents building all the software, who’s establishing the trust that we can trust this model to do work in Java or something, who’s validating the MCP servers, who’s reviewing the code if that’s something that you want to do, that sort of thing. So, we’re saving the people who are no longer writing the code, but managing and orchestrating these agents. It was a very dense video.

Nick Vidal: Yeah, we should write a book about that, about the video. Wonderful. We all know about the economic value of open source, right? There’s a study that puts the economic value of open source at $ 8.8 trillion. Open source creates enormous economic value. Yet much of the infrastructure is maintained by people and organizations that don’t receive anything close to the to the proportional value in return. Why has this model survived for so long?

First, I’d say it’s much more than $ 8.8 trillion, although it’s hard to know. It’s educated guesswork at this point. It’s not just the value of the software and what it does. Open source is a giant global community. I like to view it as a giant academic institution. There are 100 million alumni on GitHub, let’s say. All of us go out into the world and produce value for society. That adds up to a lot more than $ 8.8 trillion. The reason this model has survived is because we’re here and because we need code to do things. We need to get together in groups to face shared challenges.

It’s easier to do that with someone next to you. It starts with software, but it doesn’t end with software. You have probably half a dozen to a dozen different open movements right now that all stem from the same open source philosophy: Let’s build in public. Let’s work together. We all have shared challenges. Let’s solve them together. That’s never going to go away.

Nick Vidal: So, who should actually pay for open source? Companies, governments, foundations, users, or a combination of everyone?

Jonathan Starr: Raise your hands. Companies. Governments, foundations, users

The foundation. [Laughter] Well, I think foundations

Jonathan Starr:Let’s dig into that. So, almost everyone said companies, I think. Does anyone think companies shouldn’t pay?

I think whoever wants to should pay. That’s what it’s all about, right? It’s not centralized.

They should all pay for it.

[Laughter]

Do we all agree that someone should be paying and that money should exist in the ecosystem?

Yeah. Yes.

Ideally, open source is a byproduct of your original job. People that created open source back in the ’80s and ’90s, before it was called open source, saw free software like this: “I’ve got to do this work. Part of my work is creating something others can benefit from. I might as well post it so others can use it.” So it was a byproduct. There was a business model around open source. I would say if you’re going to use open source, you should kick in time, money, or something to support the thing you’re using. If only for your own benefit because then you’ll be an active participant in the direction of the project.

What happens when it becomes a burden on the individual who first created a thing as a side project but now so that they could become an entrepreneur a different face on a magazine and they’re more interested in a business model developing source and developing a source to solve a problem and solve very much problem it’s a profile drill and yeah yeah I do feel like everything’s becoming commodified so I do point to like what at what point does stop becoming like a passive project and it eventually devolves into like something just to make money by itself. [Unclear.] Any other thoughts?

It’s I thought the byproduct of your day were not something I thought about for a long time. But yeah, the first open source project I used was definitely a DSL driver published by a French person to work for Alcatel and they needed it for their Linux system, so they put it on the web. And as for what happens when you stop maintaining it, it’s just dead when that person is done.

So what happens when the death of that project cascades through the ecosystem and our society, our digital society kind of depends on that project continuing to work?

Engage in passion work to have a really high level of burnout. So if you want to have a ecosystem that’s healthy, you don’t have this high turnover rate, you have to compensate people. [Unclear.]

I just think there are so many different types of open source projects. So it’s like procuring it for RNG. I think I think more importantly is like how are we as books creators and like Yeah. And so that’s not exactly the right word. Are the stewards of the project like how are we responsibilities for like this this graph work? And so I think it’s I think I don’t think there’s one answer to be sure question and then more about how do we how do we shift to being more responsible as a collective or a resource. Maybe we need to find what go.

I just want to counteract some of the stuff they said over there. I feel that because of what open source has become now is so night and day different from what it was when it first became a thing. Like back when our first use open source is a world of big difference between everything used for now. Like back then might been truly that help somebody small to use this now all resources now you can almost every so it also counteract yeah it’s not almost it is used in every it’s no longer just to fix a printer sort of thing then cut

I mean there has already been like initiatives from like certain companies that understand that we live in like if anybody remembers that xkcd comic where it’s just like the entire modern internet is built off of like a Jenga tower and like the one the one small Jenga tower was like a developer in like 2005 maintaining this tirelessly for like 20 for like 20 years but I mean there has been initiatives like like Cisco contributing to like OpenSSL Well, or I think Red Hat has like the Project Lighthouse initiative where they’re they’re putting serious like time, energy, and like employee employee man hours to secure like supply chain security because that’s now a massive issue with AI. So I mean ultimately companies really really do benefit for prop having like a really strong open source ecosystem, and if they’re using it, they should contribute to it.

Jonathan Starr: We’ll come back to you in a second. To go back to what we’re defining, there’s a huge gulf in what we call open source. You can still have these passion projects and they’re amazing. I work on a distributed computing project it’s called Lettuce Compute. Come join me. Then there’s like the infrastructure of digital societies that have been recognized by many nations around the world. It’s critical to operations of a nation of a government of a society that are now starting to push like SBOMs and sort of verifying what software you depend on. So they as a government entity can sustain it. So I think it was said before like everyone in some way should be contributing to this stuff. It’s a commons. It’s a global commons. We all need to give back when we can and when we’re able. Some people are more able with money, other people with time, other people with communication, other people just answering questions in a room where we’re talking about how good we’re all facing.

Jonathan Starr: So the one of the reasons we set up the endowment, it’s me and a couple other people is because we think we as a community should have some money to give to ourselves. For so many years, we’ve been asking other people to give us money, corporations, governments, etc. And that’s all great and it’s starting to work well, which is really cool to see. But we should also have our own money to give ourselves. We are the world’s largest academic institution. We produce more IP more economic output than any other institution in the world if I want to be hyperbolic and I do. So why can Harvard have an endowment but not us. So if we view ourselves as an academic institution which is how we did it when we set up the endowment let’s give ourselves some money and let’s use the returns of those an endowment essentially you have a pot of money you invest it and you use only the returns to fund your mission our mission is open source so the idea here is over the next 100 or 200 years when as I know it’s a weird time frame to think like that but these university endowments have been around for much longer like the first endowment was hundreds and hundreds and years ago over the next 100 or 200 years we should have enough money to sustain ourselves or at least give ourselves a seat at the table during these conversations at the national level with a little bit of leverage on the financial element. We have a huge point of leverage on the community already. We are giant impactful community money also helps. [Unclear.]

I have a question. I think one of the challenges is how you assign value when deciding what to fund. There’s a lot of work out there. How does the foundation make those decisions?

Jonathan Starr: The way it’s stood up now is it’s a well first of all the initiative is very data driven so there there are data points you can get about various projects and then you can analyze them in various ways so we developed a model version 0.1 or whatever you want to call it where we just got what we could get and we analyze it how we could analyze it and that gives us a list of projects that are ranked based on that we use PageRank among some other things for this round and from that list there’s then human sort of oversight and human decision on on top of that, but we follow the data as best we can. That said, data is limiting and data changes over time. The model is open source and we would love for people to come in and kick it, break it, figure out what we should use for our next round to determine what projects are deserving of funding. Many projects deserve funding. There’s a limited amount of money to go around, and we have to make a choice.

Nick Vidal: So how do we make that choice? That’s a great segue to the next question. What exactly should we be funding? Maintainers, security, infrastructure, governance, community, or something else?

Jonathan Starr: Yes. Yes. Yes. Yes. So I think this goes up to what we were talking about when we were finding a video of what is the future of open source. It’s I don’t think it’s going to be writing code or syntax. I think it’s going to be stewarding agents, orchestrating agents, developing skills, approving skills, verifying and validating the software that is running is doing what it says it’s running in some form or another. I think we’re going to be funding groups of individuals who are doing these activities based on their domain expertise.
